hero.name: Shalini
hero.who: a chemistry teacher in Lucknow who says yes to everything and finishes nothing that matters

story.h: A full diary, an empty page
story.b: Shalini's diary is full every single day. She teaches four chemistry classes, coordinates the science exhibition, sits on the annual day committee, runs the staff welfare fund and is helping her cousin plan a wedding in Kanpur. In the evenings, she checks notebooks till midnight. Her daughter Tanvi is in Class 12 and keeps asking for help with organic chemistry. Shalini always promises Sunday. Sunday fills up too. In her cupboard sits a half-written chemistry workbook she started three years ago, her real dream. One night, she counts: eleven commitments this month and not one hour for the workbook or for Tanvi. She feels busy all the time, yet nothing important seems to move.

ask.q: Shalini has eleven commitments and none of her real priorities is moving. What should she do first?
o: Wake up earlier to fit in all eleven
Pick the few things that truly matter this term and protect them
Push through this term and sort things out during the summer vacation
ask.why: Waking earlier just stretches her thinner across eleven things, and summer will bring its own pile. Choosing the few that matter most, like Tanvi's exam year and the workbook, gives them real effort, so she can make actual progress instead of merely feeling busy.

chapters.take: Being busy is not the same as moving what matters.

story.b: Shalini writes three things on a sticky note and puts it on the fridge. Tanvi's board year. Her own classes. Two chapters of the workbook by March. Everything else, she decides, has to earn its place. She hands the welfare fund to a colleague who had asked for it last year. She tells the annual day committee she will help only in the final week. It feels strange, almost selfish. But in the first fortnight, she sits with Tanvi for an hour every evening on reaction mechanisms, and Tanvi's test marks begin to climb. On Saturday morning, Shalini writes four pages of the workbook. Doing fewer things, she does each of them far better.

ask.q: Her colleague Neelam has joined five school committees and feels completely lost. What would help her most?
o: Choose the one or two that matter most and step back from the rest
Join one more, since being seen helps her career
Stay in all five but give each a little less effort
ask.why: Another committee spreads her even thinner, and a little effort everywhere gives weak results everywhere. Picking the one or two that matter most lets her give them full attention and make real progress, which helps both her work and her peace of mind.

chapters.take: Do fewer things, and do each of them well.

story.b: The principal asks Shalini to lead a new inter-school quiz, with practice every Sunday morning. Her first instinct is to say yes, as always. Then she thinks of the note on the fridge. Sunday morning is her workbook time, the only quiet hours in her week. She realises that saying yes to the quiz means saying no to the workbook for at least three months. Nobody would see that second no. It would just happen quietly, the way the workbook has been silently pushed aside for three years. For the first time, she sees the choice clearly. It is not quiz or nothing. It is quiz or her dream. That changes how Shalini thinks about her answer.

ask.q: Shalini's neighbour says yes to every weekend function and keeps missing her own painting class. What would help her choose better?
o: Say yes to everything, since refusing hurts relationships
Skip the painting class, since it is only a hobby
Before each yes, name what it will cost her, like the painting class
ask.why: Saying yes to everything hides the cost, and calling the class only a hobby lets other people's plans decide her life. Naming what each yes will take away turns a reflex into a real choice, so she picks on purpose instead of drifting.

chapters.take: Every yes quietly says no to something else.

story.h: Let me check and tell you
story.b: In the staff room, a colleague asks Shalini to take over the eco club for the rest of the year. Everyone is watching. Before, Shalini would have said yes on the spot just to avoid an awkward moment. This time she smiles and says she will check and reply tomorrow. That night, at home, she thinks properly. Does the eco club fit her three priorities? Not really. Does she have the time? No. Would she be doing it well, or just doing it? She would be doing it badly. A day ago, the request felt impossible to refuse. Now, with a little space, the answer is clear and calm, and she no longer feels pushed into it.

ask.q: Tanvi's friend is asked to join a weekend business club and feels she must answer immediately. What is the best move?
o: Say yes now, since refusing on the spot feels rude
Ask for a day to think, then check if it fits her priorities
Say no instantly to protect her time
ask.why: An instant yes comes from pressure, not choice, and an instant no may refuse something genuinely good. Asking for a day creates space to check whether it really fits her priorities, so her final answer is thoughtful either way.

chapters.take: A small pause turns a reflex into a real choice.

story.b: An old college friend calls Shalini with a big offer. She is starting a weekend coaching centre in Aliganj and wants Shalini as her partner, teaching every Saturday and Sunday. It is flattering, and saying no to a dear friend feels terrible. But Shalini knows it would swallow the workbook and Tanvi's study hours. So she thanks her friend warmly and says how proud she is of the plan. Then she says clearly that she cannot take it on this year. She offers something smaller: she will share her chemistry notes and recommend a bright young teacher from her school. Her friend is quiet for a moment, then thanks her. The friendship feels just as warm as before.

ask.q: Shalini's friend Rekha must refuse her brother-in-law's request to manage his shop every weekend. What is the best way?
o: Say yes reluctantly and quietly resent it
Avoid his calls until he stops asking
Thank him warmly, decline clearly, and offer a smaller kind of help
ask.why: A reluctant yes breeds resentment, and dodging calls damages trust more than a clear answer would. Separating the decision from the person, staying warm, saying no clearly and offering something small protects both her time and the relationship.

chapters.take: A warm, clear no often earns more respect than a reluctant yes.

story.b: By late January, Shalini notices she is snapping at Tanvi and making small mistakes in her lesson plans. She has been checking notebooks till one in the morning. A tired mind, she realises, says yes to everything and does nothing well. So she sets a bedtime of 10.30 and treats it like a class she cannot miss. She checks notebooks in the free period after lunch instead. She also keeps Wednesday evenings empty, a buffer for whatever goes wrong. The very next week, Tanvi's school moves the practical exam date, and the Wednesday buffer absorbs it without chaos. Shalini also starts a short walk in the colony park after dinner. Her patience comes back first.

ask.q: Tanvi plans to study till 2 am every night before her boards. What should Shalini advise?
o: Keep a fixed bedtime and steady routine, since a rested mind studies better
Study till 2 am, since sleep can wait until after exams
Drink extra tea and stay up late on weekends too
ask.why: Cutting sleep may feel like extra study time, but a tired mind often focuses poorly and makes careless errors. Extra tea only hides the tiredness. A steady bedtime and routine keep her sharp enough to make good use of her study hours.

chapters.take: Rest is not laziness. It keeps you sharp enough to choose well.

story.b: Weeks later, Tanvi walks out of her chemistry board exam smiling. She says the organic questions felt familiar, almost easy. At home, on Shalini's desk, two finished chapters of the workbook sit in a neat folder, the first real progress in three years. Shalini still teaches, still helps with the annual day in its final week and still visits her cousin in Kanpur. But her diary looks different now. It has empty spaces, a bedtime and a Wednesday buffer. When the principal asks her to lead next year's quiz, she says she will think and reply on Monday. The sticky note on the fridge has faded a little. She has not needed to read it for weeks.

chapters.take: Choosing less, on purpose, makes room for what truly matters.
